ex.title: Three times more likely? How I checked a viral claim
ex.passage:
Last Tuesday a post appeared in almost every class group chat at our school. Under a photo of a teenager asleep on a pile of textbooks, it read: 'New study: teens who use their phones after 10 pm are THREE TIMES more likely to fail their exams. Share before it's too late!' Within an hour, my own parents had forwarded it to me twice.

My first instinct was to read the post carefully. Instead, I tried what professional fact-checkers do: I stopped, and before reading any further I asked who was behind the claim. The post named its source as the Brightwell Institute for Healthy Screens, which sounded official. Its website was impressive, with a logo, a list of 'research partners' and an 'About us' page describing it as 'an independent voice for digital well-being'.

But a site's description of itself is not evidence that it is reliable, so I opened a new tab and searched for the institute's name. Within five minutes, a business directory and two local news articles told me that the institute is funded by a company that sells an app to block phones at night. That does not make its claim false, but it does mean that the institute has a vested interest in alarming parents.

Next, I looked for better coverage. If a study had really found such a dramatic effect, I would expect established newspapers or health services to have reported it. I could not find a single one that had.

Finally, I traced the claim to its origin. The institute's report turned out to be an online survey of 214 users of the company's own app. They were asked how often they used their phones after 10 pm and whether their last exam results had been 'worse than expected'. The phrase 'three times more likely' did not appear in the report at all. It came from a press release that compared only the heaviest night-time users with the lightest, and nobody in the survey had been asked whether they had actually failed an exam.

So is the claim false? Not entirely. Other research, published in peer-reviewed journals, suggests that late-night phone use can cut into sleep, and that poor sleep can affect learning. The direction of the post may be reasonable; its number is not supported by anything I could find.

What I learnt is that checking a source and checking a claim are two separate jobs. An unreliable source can repeat something true, and a reliable source can get things wrong. Lateral reading tells you whom to trust. It does not tell you what is true.

questions.question: What did the writer do first, instead of reading the post carefully?
options: Read the institute's 'About us' page to learn about its research.
Shared it with a warning that it might be false.
Stopped and asked who was behind the claim.
Emailed the researchers to ask for their data.

0.en: The writer looked at the page, but explains that a site's description of itself is not evidence of reliability.

1.en: The writer did not share it: the first SIFT move is to stop before sharing.

3.en: The article does not mention contacting anyone.

explanation.en: 'I stopped, and before reading any further I asked who was behind the claim': the S of SIFT.

questions.question: Why was the institute's 'About us' page not enough to show that it was reliable?
options: Because it was written by the institute itself.
Because it contained spelling mistakes.
Because it did not list any research partners.
Because the website had no logo.

1.en: The article does not mention spelling mistakes.

2.en: The site did list 'research partners'; a list like that is also written by the site.

3.en: It did have a logo, and the writer's point is that a logo proves nothing.

explanation.en: 'A site's description of itself is not evidence that it is reliable', so she checked what other sources said about it: lateral reading.

questions.statement: The writer concludes that the claim must be false because of who funds the institute.

explanation.en: 'That does not make its claim false, but it does mean that the institute has a vested interest.' Funding tells you how cautious to be, not whether the claim is true.

questions.text: Because the institute is funded by a company that sells a night-time blocking app, it has a ___ interest in alarming parents.

explanation.en: The article's word is vested: a vested interest is a personal, often financial, reason to want a particular result.

questions.question: Where did the figure 'three times more likely' come from?
options: From a large, peer-reviewed study that followed students' phone use for a year
From comparing the official exam results of the 214 people in the survey
From a survey question that asked people whether they had failed an exam
From a press release that compared only the heaviest and the lightest night-time users

0.en: The report was an online survey of the company's own app users, not a peer-reviewed study.

1.en: No official results were used: people said only whether their last results had been 'worse than expected'.

2.en: Nobody was asked whether they had actually failed an exam.

explanation.en: Tracing the claim showed that the number came from a press release comparing two extreme groups, not from the report itself.

questions.question: Which weaknesses of the original survey does the article mention?
options: It took too long to complete and would be too expensive for anyone else to repeat.
It surveyed only the company's own app users and asked about results 'worse than expected', not about failing.
It was published in an expensive journal, so the writer could read only a summary of it.
It included too many students from the writer's own school and too few from other areas.

0.en: Length and cost are not mentioned.

2.en: The report was not in a journal; the writer found and read it.

3.en: The article does not say who the 214 app users were, apart from being the company's customers.

explanation.en: The sample was self-selected (app customers), and the outcome measured ('worse than expected') was not the outcome claimed (failing exams).

questions.statement: The writer accepts that late-night phone use may affect learning.

explanation.en: 'Other research ... suggests that late-night phone use can cut into sleep, and that poor sleep can affect learning. The direction of the post may be reasonable.'

questions.question: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Professional fact-checkers are more reliable than scientists when it comes to judging research.
Phone use after 10 pm has no real effect on exam results, whatever the post claims.
Checking whether a source is reliable and checking whether a claim is true are different jobs.
Students should never share posts about research, because most of them turn out to be false.

0.en: The writer uses fact-checkers' methods but does not compare them with scientists.

1.en: The writer says the direction of the claim may be reasonable.

3.en: The point is to check before sharing, not to stop sharing altogether; the writer never claims that most posts are false.

explanation.en: 'An unreliable source can repeat something true, and a reliable source can get things wrong. Lateral reading tells you whom to trust. It does not tell you what is true.'

prompt.en: Read the opinion column from a local newspaper (an invented example about a fictional town). Some of its reasoning is flawed and some is sound. Answer the questions.

ex.title: It is time to ban e-scooters from Larkfield
ex.passage:
Two years ago, Larkfield allowed rental e-scooters on its streets. Since then, the number of people treated at Larkfield General Hospital for minor injuries has risen every year, and residents have complained more and more about speeding riders. The connection could not be clearer: the scooters are making our town more dangerous, and the council must ban them before someone is killed.

I have seen the danger myself. Last month my neighbour's son was thrown from a scooter outside the station and broke his wrist, and a week later a rider almost knocked over an elderly woman on Mill Road. Anyone who walks through the town centre knows that scooter riders simply do not care about pedestrians.

The scooter company, of course, disagrees. Its local manager told this newspaper that most riders use the scooters safely. But what would you expect him to say? He is a twenty-six-year-old who has probably never had to push a pram along a crowded pavement. Supporters of the scheme, meanwhile, seem to believe that our pavements should be turned into racetracks for anyone with an app.

There is also a practical problem that deserves attention. Scooters are often left lying across pavements, and for wheelchair users or people with poor eyesight, a scooter dropped in the wrong place can block a route completely. Disability groups have been raising this with the council for months, and they have yet to receive a reply. This is not just a matter of opinion: anyone can see scooters lying across the pavement on Station Road on a weekday morning, and the council's own complaints log will show how often the problem has been reported.

Some councillors suggest new rules instead: lower speed limits, parking zones and fines for riding on pavements. But rules like these will only be the beginning. If we accept scooters with speed limits today, tomorrow it will be electric bikes on pavements, then skateboards, and before long no pedestrian in Larkfield will be safe.

The choice is simple. Either we ban scooters now, or we accept that our pavements will belong to them. In our online poll last week, a large majority of readers voted for a ban. When that many people agree, the council has no excuse to wait.

questions.question: What is wrong with the reasoning in paragraph 1?
options: It assumes the scooters caused the rise in injuries just because the rise came after they arrived.
It attacks the hospital staff instead of examining their figures.
It relies on a story about a single accident to support a claim about the whole town.
It quotes a hospital doctor who is not an expert on road safety.

1.en: The hospital staff are not criticised at all.

2.en: The single accident appears in paragraph 2, not paragraph 1.

3.en: Nobody is quoted in paragraph 1.

explanation.en: Post hoc: the writer never shows that the minor injuries involved scooters at all. The town may have grown, or more people may be cycling or doing sport. 'The connection could not be clearer' is asserted, not demonstrated.

questions.question: Which sentence in paragraph 2 is a hasty generalisation?
options: I have seen the danger myself.
Last month my neighbour's son was thrown from a scooter outside the station and broke his wrist.
Anyone who walks through the town centre knows that scooter riders simply do not care about pedestrians.
A week later a rider almost knocked over an elderly woman on Mill Road.

0.en: This introduces the writer's experience; it does not yet generalise.

1.en: This reports one incident. Anecdotes are not fallacies in themselves; the problem is the conclusion drawn from them.

3.en: This is a second anecdote. The fallacy is the leap from two incidents to all riders.

explanation.en: Two incidents become a claim about all scooter riders ('simply do not care'), backed only by 'anyone ... knows'. A sound version would say that these incidents show a risk worth investigating.

questions.question: How does the writer respond to the manager's claim that most riders use the scooters safely?
options: By presenting evidence that most riders are unsafe.
By questioning the manager's age and experience instead of his claim.
By agreeing with the manager and dropping the call for a ban.
By noting his vested interest and then checking his figures against independent data.

0.en: No evidence about riders in general is given.

2.en: The writer still calls for a ban at the end of the column.

3.en: Noting a vested interest would be fair, but the writer never checks any figures: the claim is dismissed because of who made it.

explanation.en: 'What would you expect him to say?' could lead to a fair check of his claim, but the writer turns instead to his age and imagined experience. That is ad hominem: it says nothing about whether most riders are safe.

questions.statement: The writer describes the supporters' view in a way that they would probably accept.

explanation.en: Supporters are said to want pavements 'turned into racetracks for anyone with an app': a straw man. Their likely argument (cheap, low-emission short journeys) is never stated.

questions.question: Which paragraph makes a reasonable point that the writer could build a sound argument on?
options: Paragraph 1
Paragraph 3
Paragraph 4
Paragraph 6

0.en: Paragraph 1 rests on a false-cause leap.

1.en: Paragraph 3 attacks the manager and caricatures supporters.

3.en: Paragraph 6 relies on a false dilemma and an appeal to popularity.

explanation.en: Paragraph 4 identifies a specific, checkable harm (scooters blocking routes for wheelchair users and people with poor eyesight) and a real failure to respond. Not every point in a flawed text is a fallacy.

questions.question: What would the writer need in order to make paragraph 5 a sound argument?
options: More emotional language about the dangers to pedestrians on crowded pavements
Evidence for each step in the chain, for example from towns that introduced similar rules
A larger online poll showing that even more readers are worried about the change
A quotation from a well-known local figure who agrees with the column

0.en: Stronger feelings do not support a prediction.

2.en: A poll shows what readers think, not what will happen if speed limits are introduced.

3.en: Fame is not expertise, and agreement is not evidence.

explanation.en: Paragraph 5 is a slippery slope: speed limits → electric bikes on pavements → skateboards → nobody safe. A chain of predictions is only as strong as the evidence for each link.

questions.question: Which sentence best repairs the false dilemma in the final paragraph?
options: The choice is simple: either we ban scooters this year, or we accept that our pavements will soon belong to them for good.
Most readers who voted in our poll want a ban, so a ban is the only option that the council can now consider.
Anyone who still does not support a ban, after everything that has happened, simply does not care about pedestrians.
The council has three realistic options (a ban, stricter rules with parking zones, or a trial of those rules) and should compare them on safety and cost.

0.en: This repeats the false dilemma.

1.en: This replaces one fallacy with another: popularity does not make an option the only one.

2.en: This adds an ad hominem attack on opponents.

explanation.en: The repair names the realistic options, including a middle way, and sets criteria for choosing between them. The writer could still argue for a ban, but would have to show why it beats the alternatives.

questions.text: Using a readers' poll as proof that a ban is the right decision is an appeal to ___.

explanation.en: An appeal to popularity: the poll shows what many readers want, not whether a ban would work. It is also an online poll, so its readers chose to take part.

prompt.en: Read the opinion column from a local newspaper and answer the questions.

ex.title: Two leaflets, one doormat
ex.passage:
This week two leaflets landed on my doormat, one from each side of the referendum on the old rail yard. Should the land become a public park, or should the council sell it for new homes? I have not made up my mind, and I suspect many readers have not either. So rather than tell you how to vote, I want to look at how each side is trying to win your vote.

The Yes to the Park leaflet opens with a photograph of a small child staring through a wire fence at the empty yard. Underneath, in large letters, it asks: 'Do you want your grandchildren to grow up surrounded by concrete?' It is an effective question, but it is not a fair one. Nobody is proposing to cover the town in concrete; the housing plan itself includes a garden square. The question works by making you say 'no' to something that is not on the ballot.

Turn the leaflet over, however, and the tone changes. The campaign points out that the nearest park is a forty-minute walk for families on the eastern estates, sets out a costed plan for maintaining the new one, and admits that 'a park will not solve the housing shortage'. That last sentence is the most persuasive thing in the leaflet. A campaign that tells you what its plan cannot do gives you a reason to believe what it says the plan can do.

The Homes First leaflet runs the other way: it starts strong and then lets itself down. Its central argument is serious: young couples are leaving the town because they cannot afford the rent, and two hundred new flats would ease the pressure. It even offers a memorable line: 'A park is somewhere to visit; a home is somewhere to live.' That sentence does real work, because it names the choice at the heart of the vote. But the leaflet then claims that 'everyone under thirty supports Homes First' and describes the park campaigners as 'a few retired people with large gardens'. The first claim is impossible to check and almost certainly untrue; the second is a sneer, not an argument. Both will please readers who already agree, and both will put off the undecided voters the campaign most needs.

What strikes me is that the strongest parts of each leaflet are the least dramatic: a walking distance, a cost, an honest admission, a clear statement of the trade-off. The weakest parts are the ones that try hardest to make me feel something without giving me a reason to feel it.

I will vote next month, and I still do not know which way. But I know what kind of argument I will be listening for.

questions.question: What is the columnist's main purpose?
options: To persuade readers to vote for the park
To argue that the town should not have held a referendum
To criticise the Homes First campaign only
To show readers how to judge the way each side argues

0.en: The columnist has 'not made up my mind' and both praises and criticises each leaflet.

1.en: The columnist never questions the referendum itself.

2.en: The park leaflet is criticised too, for its opening question.

explanation.en: 'Rather than tell you how to vote, I want to look at how each side is trying to win your vote.' The column evaluates rhetoric, not policy.

questions.question: Why does the columnist call the park leaflet's opening question 'not a fair one'?
options: It asks readers to reject an outcome that nobody is actually proposing.
Questions should never be used in political leaflets.
It does not mention how much the park would cost.
The photograph of the child was not taken in this town.

1.en: The columnist calls it 'an effective question'; the problem is what it implies, not the fact that it is a question.

2.en: The cost is set out on the back of the leaflet, and the columnist praises it.

3.en: The text says nothing about where the photograph was taken.

explanation.en: 'Nobody is proposing to cover the town in concrete ... The question works by making you say no to something that is not on the ballot.' A rhetorical question is unfair when it smuggles in a false picture of the choice.

questions.statement: The columnist thinks the park campaign's admission that 'a park will not solve the housing shortage' weakens its case.

explanation.en: 'That last sentence is the most persuasive thing in the leaflet.' Admitting a limit builds credibility (ethos).

questions.question: 'A park is somewhere to visit; a home is somewhere to live.' Which device is this?
options: A rhetorical question
A tricolon
An antithesis
A concession

0.en: It is a statement, not a question.

1.en: A tricolon has three parallel parts; this sentence has two.

3.en: It grants nothing to the other side; it sharpens a contrast.

explanation.en: Two contrasting ideas in a parallel structure (somewhere to visit / somewhere to live): an antithesis. It 'does real work' because the contrast names the real choice in the vote.

questions.question: The description of the park campaigners as 'a few retired people with large gardens' is best described as ...
options: a fair summary of the other side's view
an attack on the people instead of their argument
a piece of evidence that readers can check
a carefully hedged claim

0.en: It says nothing about what park campaigners actually argue; it mocks who they are.

2.en: It cannot be checked, and it does not support the case for housing.

3.en: There is no hedge here; 'a few' is dismissive, not cautious.

explanation.en: The columnist calls it 'a sneer, not an argument'. It is an ad hominem move: it targets the people, not their reasons, and it works only on readers who already agree.

questions.statement: The columnist states that the claim 'everyone under thirty supports Homes First' is definitely false.

explanation.en: The columnist says it is 'impossible to check and almost certainly untrue': a strong but hedged judgement, not 'definitely false'. Read hedges as carefully as you write them.

questions.text: According to the columnist, the strongest parts of both leaflets are the least ___. (one word from the column)

feedback.en: Close in meaning, but the columnist's word is 'dramatic': the strongest parts are 'the least dramatic'.
The opposite: these parts are the most persuasive. The columnist's word is 'dramatic'.

explanation.en: '... the strongest parts of each leaflet are the least dramatic: a walking distance, a cost, an honest admission, a clear statement of the trade-off.'

prompt.en: Read the column by a university writing tutor and answer the questions.

ex.title: Cut, cut, cut? Not quite
ex.passage:
Every year, my first-year students hand in essays that are too long in the wrong places and too short in the right ones. The introduction spends a hundred words announcing what the essay will do; the paragraph that should carry the argument gets three sentences and no example. The fix is rarely more writing. It is better editing.

The most common advice about editing is 'cut, cut, cut'. It is half right. Most first drafts are full of words that do no work: 'due to the fact that' where 'because' would do, 'in my personal opinion, I think' in an essay that is already the writer's opinion, 'a total of twelve students' where 'twelve students' says the same. Removing this padding makes a text faster to read, and it makes the writer sound more confident. But a writer who cuts everything that looks like padding will also cut things that are not. 'Many' is not padding when the alternative is 'all'. 'In this sample' is not padding when the study was small. 'However' is not padding when it warns the reader that the next sentence pulls against the last. Concision means removing words that add nothing, not words that add caution, logic or evidence.

Precision matters as much as length. 'The policy affected attendance' is short, but it hides the one thing the reader wants to know: did attendance rise or fall, and by how much? 'Attendance fell slightly in the first term' is longer and better. Vague verbs (affect, deal with, look at) and vague nouns (things, issues, aspects) spare the writer the effort of deciding what they mean. Replacing them forces that decision, which is why precise wording improves the thinking as well as the prose.

The stage students skip is proofreading. By the time they reach it, they are tired of the essay, and they read what they meant to write rather than what is on the page. I ask them to change the format first, by printing the essay or switching to a different font, and then to read it aloud, slowly. A missing article or a doubled word slips past the eye far more easily than past the ear.

None of this is glamorous. Nobody remembers an essay because its writer deleted 'it is important to note that' eleven times. But readers notice, even if they cannot say why, when every sentence earns its place. That is what a second draft is for.

questions.question: What is the tutor's view of the advice 'cut, cut, cut'?
options: It is partly right: cutting padding helps, but cutting hedges, connectors and evidence does harm.
It is the best single piece of advice a writer can follow.
It is wrong, because longer essays usually receive higher marks.
It applies only to introductions, not to body paragraphs.

1.en: 'It is half right': the tutor warns that cutting too much removes caution, logic and evidence.

2.en: The tutor never links length to marks; the complaint is about words in the wrong places.

3.en: Padding can appear anywhere; the tutor's examples are not limited to introductions.

explanation.en: 'It is half right ... Concision means removing words that add nothing, not words that add caution, logic or evidence.'

questions.question: Why is 'many' not padding 'when the alternative is all'?
options: Because 'many' is shorter than 'all'
Because 'all' is too informal for an essay
Because readers prefer vague words
Because 'many' limits the claim to what the evidence can support

0.en: 'Many' is actually longer than 'all'; the point is about meaning, not length.

1.en: 'All' is not informal; the problem is that it may over-claim.

2.en: The tutor argues for precision, not vagueness.

explanation.en: 'Many' sets the scope of the claim. Removing it, or changing it to 'all', would turn an accurate claim into an over-generalisation: the calibration you practised in the hedging lesson.

questions.statement: The tutor prefers 'Attendance fell slightly in the first term' to 'The policy affected attendance', even though it is longer.

explanation.en: '... is longer and better.' Precision can justify extra words, because they tell the reader what actually happened.

questions.statement: According to the tutor, replacing vague words improves the style of an essay but not its ideas.

explanation.en: The tutor says precise wording 'improves the thinking as well as the prose', because it forces the writer to decide what they mean.

questions.question: According to the tutor, why do students miss errors when they proofread?
options: They proofread before they have finished the argument.
They read what they meant to write rather than what is on the page.
They rely too much on spell-checkers.
They proofread on paper instead of on screen.

0.en: The tutor describes proofreading as the last stage, the one that students skip, not one they do too early.

2.en: Spell-checkers are not mentioned.

3.en: The opposite: the tutor recommends printing the essay.

explanation.en: '... they read what they meant to write rather than what is on the page.' Changing the format and reading aloud help to break that habit.

questions.text: The tutor suggests changing the ___ of the essay, for example by printing it, before reading it aloud. (one word from the column)

feedback.en: Switching the font is one example of the change. The general word in the column is 'format'.

explanation.en: 'I ask them to change the format first, by printing the essay or switching to a different font, and then to read it aloud, slowly.'

questions.question: Which sentence best summarises the column?
options: Short essays are always better than long ones.
Students should spend more time on their introductions.
Good editing cuts words that add nothing, sharpens vague wording and checks the final text closely, while keeping every word that adds meaning.
Proofreading matters more than any other stage of writing.

0.en: The tutor says concision is not the same as brevity: 'Attendance fell slightly ...' is longer and better.

1.en: The tutor criticises introductions that spend 'a hundred words announcing what the essay will do'.

3.en: Proofreading is one stage among several; the column gives equal weight to concision and precision.

explanation.en: The column covers three stages (cutting padding, choosing precise words, proofreading) and one principle: every sentence should earn its place.

prompt.en: Read the column by a newspaper's readers' editor and answer the questions.

ex.title: The words we didn't notice
ex.passage:
Last Thursday, this paper reported on a protest outside the town hall against the planned closure of the Riverside swimming pool. By Friday morning I had received forty-one complaints. Not one of them disputed a fact. The number of people present, the time, the route of the march and the words on the banners were all accurate. What readers objected to was the vocabulary.

Our report said that 'a crowd of around three hundred' had 'gathered' outside the building. Several readers who support the closure wrote to say that 'gathered' made a noisy demonstration sound like a picnic. Readers on the other side were no happier. They pointed out that the council's plan, which our headline called a closure, is described in the council's own documents as 'a rationalisation of leisure provision', and that we had quoted this phrase twice without comment. One reader asked whether we would describe a fire as an unplanned rationalisation of the building.

Both groups have a point, and it is the same point: there is no neutral vocabulary waiting to be used. Every word carries connotations, the associations that cling to it beyond its dictionary meaning. 'Crowd' is calmer than 'mob'; 'gathered' is gentler than 'massed'; 'rationalisation' is a euphemism that makes a loss sound like tidying up. A reporter cannot avoid connotation. She can only choose it, and she should choose it consciously.

Our style guide offers a simple test: would both sides accept this word as a fair description, even if they would not choose it themselves? 'Crowd' passes; 'mob' does not. 'Closure' passes, because that is what will happen to the building. 'Rationalisation' fails, unless it appears in quotation marks and is clearly attributed to the council. On that test, our report was mostly fair, and our use of the council's phrase was not.

There was a second, subtler complaint. A retired teacher noted that the paragraph about the protesters was written in long, winding sentences full of qualifications, while the paragraph quoting the council's spokesperson was short, crisp and confident. 'You gave one side the rhythm of certainty,' she wrote, 'and the other the rhythm of excuses.' I read the article again with her letter beside me. She was right, and I doubt the reporter intended it. Sentence rhythm is rarely discussed in newsrooms, but readers feel it, and it shapes their sense of who sounds reasonable.

None of this means that reporters should aim for grey, connotation-free prose. Such prose does not exist, and the attempt to produce it tends to create a dull, evasive voice that readers trust even less. What it means is that word choice is part of accuracy. A report can get every fact right and still mislead through its adjectives, its euphemisms and its cadence. We will be adding the rhythm test to our style guide.

questions.question: Why does the readers' editor point out that 'not one of them disputed a fact'?
options: To suggest that the complaints were unjustified
To show that the problem lay in the connotations of the words, not in the information reported
To prove that the reporter had checked every source carefully
To criticise readers for not reading the article carefully

0.en: She says that 'both groups have a point', so she does not dismiss the complaints.

2.en: The accuracy of the facts is the starting point, not the conclusion: the column is about what went wrong despite accurate facts.

3.en: She does not blame readers; she agrees with much of what they wrote.

explanation.en: 'What readers objected to was the vocabulary.' The facts were right; the words carried judgements.

questions.statement: The writer believes that a careful reporter can find words with no connotations at all.

explanation.en: 'There is no neutral vocabulary waiting to be used ... A reporter cannot avoid connotation. She can only choose it.'

questions.question: According to the style guide's test, when would 'rationalisation' be acceptable?
options: When it appears in quotation marks and is clearly attributed to the council
When the reporter agrees with the council's plan
When it is used in the headline rather than in the article
Never, because it is a euphemism

1.en: The test is whether both sides would accept the word as fair, not whether the reporter agrees.

2.en: The column does not distinguish headlines from articles on this point; the headline in fact used 'closure'.

3.en: Not never: 'unless it appears in quotation marks and is clearly attributed to the council'.

explanation.en: Quoting and attributing the euphemism shows that it is the council's wording, not the paper's own description.

questions.question: What does the retired teacher mean by 'the rhythm of certainty' and 'the rhythm of excuses'?
options: The council's spokesperson spoke more slowly than the protesters.
The reporter quoted the protesters more often than the council.
Short, confident sentences made the council sound reasonable, while long, qualified sentences made the protesters sound defensive.
The protesters' banners were written in a more emotional style than the council's documents.

0.en: The complaint is about how the article was written, not how anyone spoke.

1.en: Neither the number of quotations nor the balance of space is mentioned; the point is sentence length and style.

3.en: The banners are mentioned only as an accurate fact in the first paragraph.

explanation.en: The protesters' paragraph had 'long, winding sentences full of qualifications'; the council's was 'short, crisp and confident'. Rhythm shaped readers' 'sense of who sounds reasonable'.

questions.statement: The writer thinks the reporter deliberately favoured the council.

explanation.en: 'She was right, and I doubt the reporter intended it.' The bias was real but probably unconscious, which is why the paper is adding a rhythm test.

questions.text: The writer concludes that word choice is part of ___. (one word from the column)

feedback.en: The column's point is stronger than that: a report can 'get every fact right and still mislead', so word choice is part of accuracy.

explanation.en: 'What it means is that word choice is part of accuracy.'

questions.question: What is the writer's view of 'grey, connotation-free prose'?
options: It is the goal every reporter should aim for.
It is possible, but only in headlines.
It is the style the paper's style guide requires.
It does not exist, and attempting it produces an evasive voice that readers distrust.

0.en: 'None of this means that reporters should aim for grey, connotation-free prose.'

1.en: The writer says such prose 'does not exist' anywhere.

2.en: The style guide's test is about fairness to both sides, not about removing connotation.

explanation.en: 'Such prose does not exist, and the attempt to produce it tends to create a dull, evasive voice that readers trust even less.'

prompt.en: Read the editorial from a local newspaper and answer the questions.

ex.title: Congratulations are in order
ex.passage:
It is not every day that a town gets a new landmark, so let us begin by congratulating Brennock Town Council on the opening of the Millbank Footbridge. Three years later than promised and at roughly twice the agreed cost, the bridge now crosses the River Esk in an elegant curve of steel and glass. It is, by any standard, a handsome structure. It is also, by any standard, a bridge to a fence.

Readers who have not yet visited may be unaware of this detail. The footbridge carries pedestrians gracefully across the water and delivers them, after forty metres of gentle climb, to a padlocked gate at the edge of a field that the council does not own. The landowner, we understand, was first contacted about the land last spring, some two years after construction began. Negotiations are said to be 'ongoing'.

The council describes the project as 'substantially complete'. In a sense, it is: the part that cost money is finished. The part that would make it useful has not yet begun. A spokesperson told this paper that the bridge 'already offers residents a unique vantage point over the river', which is true, and that the overspend was 'within normal parameters for a project of this complexity', a sentence we have now read four times without discovering what it means.

The council's communications team, it must be said, has not been idle. In the past month residents have received a glossy leaflet, two press releases and a short film of the bridge at sunset, shot from a drone. The film is beautiful. It does not show the gate.

At the opening ceremony, the mayor thanked the engineers, the contractors and the people of Brennock for their patience. She did not mention the land. Perhaps there was not time.

We do not wish to be unfair. Large projects run into difficulties, and the engineers have built exactly what they were asked to build. Nor is the bridge entirely without value: on a clear evening it is a pleasant place to stand, and several couples have already been photographed on it. But a footbridge is not a viewing platform, and residents were promised a route to the railway station, not a view of it from behind a padlocked gate.

So, plainly: the council should commission an independent review of how the project was planned, publish it in full, and tell residents when, and at what additional cost, the bridge will lead somewhere. Until it does, the most honest name for the Millbank Footbridge is the one already used by half the town. We will not print it, but readers can probably guess.

questions.question: What is the editorial's overall position?
options: The bridge is a handsome structure, and the council deserves congratulations.
The engineers should be blamed for building a bridge that leads nowhere.
The project was badly planned, and the council should commission and publish an independent review.
The bridge should be officially turned into a viewing platform.

0.en: This takes the opening at face value. The congratulations are ironic: the next sentences list the delay, the overspend and the fence.

1.en: The writer defends the engineers: they 'have built exactly what they were asked to build'. The criticism is aimed at the planning.

3.en: 'A footbridge is not a viewing platform': the writer wants the bridge to become the route residents were promised.

explanation.en: The irony runs through the first five paragraphs, and the last paragraph states the position directly: 'So, plainly: the council should commission an independent review ... publish it in full ...'.

questions.question: The writer says they have read the spokesperson's sentence about 'normal parameters' four times 'without discovering what it means'. What does this imply?
options: The writer is not familiar with engineering terms.
The sentence contains a printing error.
The spokesperson spoke too quickly to be understood.
The sentence is evasive jargon that avoids admitting the overspend was a problem.

0.en: The pretended confusion is ironic. The writer understands perfectly well that the sentence is designed to say nothing.

1.en: Nothing suggests an error; the sentence is quoted exactly because its emptiness is the point.

2.en: The writer has 'read' the sentence, so speed of speech is irrelevant.

explanation.en: The writer breaks the expectation that a quotation is included to inform. By claiming not to understand it, the writer implies that the sentence was built to sound reassuring while avoiding any admission, a criticism made without stating it.

questions.statement: The writer believes that the council's communications team has done very little work.

explanation.en: 'Has not been idle' is litotes: the team has been very busy, producing a leaflet, two press releases and a film. The irony is that all this effort went into publicity, and the film 'does not show the gate'.

questions.question: 'She did not mention the land. Perhaps there was not time.' What do these two sentences suggest?
options: The ceremony was too short for a full speech.
The mayor avoided the subject that explains the failure, and the second sentence is ironic.
The land was not relevant to the opening of the bridge.
The mayor did not know that the council does not own the land.

0.en: 'Perhaps there was not time' is not meant literally. Placed after a list of people she found time to thank, it mocks the excuse.

2.en: The land is the whole problem: the bridge ends at a gate to a field the council does not own.

3.en: The editorial does not discuss what the mayor knew; it implies that she chose not to raise the subject.

explanation.en: The first sentence works by quantity: what the mayor left out is the most important fact. The second offers an obviously inadequate excuse, which is a form of irony. Together they accuse her of evasion without saying so.

questions.text: The writer places the council's description 'substantially ___' in quotation marks to show doubt about it. (one word from the editorial)

feedback.en: 'Ongoing' is also in quotation marks, but it describes the negotiations. The council's description of the whole project is 'substantially complete'.

explanation.en: 'The council describes the project as "substantially complete". In a sense, it is: the part that cost money is finished.' The quotation marks, and the comment that follows, distance the paper from the council's wording.

questions.statement: The final paragraph begins by dropping the irony and stating the paper's demands directly.

explanation.en: 'So, plainly:' signals the change. After paragraphs of irony, the explicit demands (commission a review, publish it, give a date and a cost) make the position unmistakable. Only the closing lines, about the bridge's unofficial name, return to humour.

questions.question: Why does the writer include the paragraph beginning 'We do not wish to be unfair'?
options: To concede fair points, which makes the criticism more credible
To withdraw the criticism made earlier in the editorial
To shift the blame from the council to the engineers
To recommend the bridge as a place for wedding photographs

1.en: The criticism continues straight after the concessions: 'But a footbridge is not a viewing platform ...'.

2.en: The paragraph defends the engineers, who 'built exactly what they were asked to build'.

3.en: The photographs are a concession that the bridge has some value, immediately qualified by 'But ...'.

explanation.en: By granting what is true (large projects run into problems; the engineers did their job; the bridge has some value), the writer shows fairness, so readers are more likely to accept the central criticism. Note the litotes again: 'Nor is the bridge entirely without value' grants very little.

prompt.en: You are writing an essay on whether towns should close their main shopping streets to private cars. Read the three extracts and answer the questions. (All three sources are invented for this exercise.)

ex.title: Three sources on car-free town centres
ex.passage:
Source A. Mizrahi, H. (2022), from an article in an academic journal
Twelve months after Easton Vale closed its high street to private cars, we surveyed the same 64 businesses that had taken part in our baseline survey; 58 of them completed both surveys. Footfall, measured by automatic counters at both ends of the street, rose throughout the year, and most cafés, restaurants and clothing shops reported higher takings. The picture was not uniform, however. Two hardware shops, whose customers typically buy heavy or bulky goods, closed during the study period, and their owners cited the loss of kerbside parking. Easton Vale is unusually well served by public transport, with buses to the centre every ten minutes, and we would caution against assuming that the same results would follow in towns without such a service. A comparison with similar towns that kept their streets open was beyond the scope of this study.

Source B. Lund, P. (2023), from an online opinion column in a local newspaper
I have sold furniture on Calder Mills high street for twenty-two years, and since the street closed to cars my sales have fallen every quarter. My customers are not the young professionals in the council's brochures. Many are older, some have mobility problems, and almost all of them need to load a car. The council tells me that footfall is up. Footfall does not buy wardrobes. A street that is pleasant to stroll down is not always a street you can shop in. I accept that the cafés have done well; on a sunny afternoon you cannot find a table. But a town centre that only works for people buying coffee is not a town centre. It is a food court with nice paving.

Source C. Northfield Transport Research Group (2023), from a research report
This report compares retail activity in six towns of similar size, all of which closed their main shopping street to private cars. The towns were matched on population and on the proportion of residents over 65, but not on average income. Eighteen months after the change, the three towns with frequent bus services to the centre (at least every fifteen minutes) had recorded rising retail activity, while the three with less frequent services had recorded falls. The pattern held across most types of shop, although businesses selling bulky goods did worse in all six towns. Because the follow-up period was short, we cannot say whether these effects will last. We recommend that towns considering a closure improve public transport first.

questions.question: Which sentence best synthesises Sources A and C?
options: Mizrahi (2022) studied Easton Vale, and the Northfield Transport Research Group (2023) studied six towns.

Mizrahi's (2022) positive findings in Easton Vale, a town with buses every ten minutes, are in line with the Northfield Transport Research Group's (2023) conclusion that retail gains depend on frequent public transport.
Both Mizrahi (2022) and the Northfield Transport Research Group (2023) prove that car-free streets help all businesses.
The Northfield Transport Research Group (2023) refutes Mizrahi's (2022) findings.

0.en: Accurate, but this is two summaries joined by 'and'. It says nothing about how the sources relate.

2.en: Over-claims twice: neither source proves anything, and both report that some businesses (hardware shops, bulky goods) did worse.

3.en: The sources do not conflict on this point: Easton Vale has frequent buses, exactly the condition under which the Northfield report found gains.

explanation.en: The synthesis connects a detail in A (buses every ten minutes) with the pattern in C (gains only where buses are frequent), so each source helps explain the other.

questions.question: Which reporting verb best describes what Lund does in the sentence 'I accept that the cafés have done well'?
options: demonstrates
disputes
concedes
speculates

0.en: Lund offers no evidence beyond an observation, and the point is not his main argument; he is granting something to the other side.

1.en: He agrees about the cafés; what he disputes is that a café-friendly street is a successful town centre.

3.en: Speculates suggests guessing. Lund states the point as something he has seen ('you cannot find a table').

explanation.en: Lund accepts a point that weakens his own case (some businesses have gained), then argues that it is not enough. That is a concession: Lund (2023) concedes that cafés have benefited, but ...

questions.statement: All three sources report that car-free streets have helped cafés.

explanation.en: Sources A and B mention cafés doing well, but Source C does not mention cafés at all, and it reports falls in three of its six towns. Claiming agreement across all your sources when only some agree is a common synthesis error.

questions.question: Which limitation do Sources A and C share?
options: Both are based on the experience of a single business.
Both studied only one town.
Neither mentions public transport.
Both measured effects over a short period, so neither can show long-term results.

0.en: That describes Source B, Lund's column about his own shop.

1.en: Only Source A studied one town; Source C compares six.

2.en: Both discuss public transport: A notes buses every ten minutes, and C's main finding concerns bus frequency.

explanation.en: A surveyed businesses after twelve months and C after eighteen, and C says directly that 'we cannot say whether these effects will last'. A shared limitation belongs in your synthesis, because it limits the conclusion you can draw from both sources.

questions.statement: Source C contains a finding that could help explain Lund's falling sales, whatever the bus service in his town.

explanation.en: C reports that 'businesses selling bulky goods did worse in all six towns', and Lund sells furniture. So his experience may be in line with the research rather than at odds with it. Noticing this is synthesis: one source helps you interpret another.

questions.text: Lund's evidence comes from his own ___, so it cannot show what happened to the town's businesses as a whole. (one word)

explanation.en: 'I have sold furniture ... my sales have fallen every quarter.' One shop's sales are a case, not a pattern. Lund's column is useful as a perspective, especially on older and disabled customers, but not as evidence about a whole street.

questions.question: Which thesis makes the best use of all three sources?
options: Closing a high street to cars can benefit many businesses, but the evidence suggests that the gains depend on frequent public transport and that shops selling bulky goods are likely to lose out.
Car-free town centres always benefit local businesses.
Mizrahi, Lund and the Northfield Transport Research Group have all written about car-free town centres.
As Lund proves, car-free town centres harm businesses.

1.en: 'Always' is contradicted by every source: hardware shops closed (A), Lund's sales fell (B), and three towns saw falls (C).

2.en: This is a description of the sources, not a claim. A thesis must say something arguable that the sources support.

3.en: One shop cannot prove a general claim, and the thesis ignores the gains reported in A and C.

explanation.en: The best thesis is qualified and draws on all three sources: gains (A, C), the condition of frequent buses (A, C) and the losers, shops selling bulky goods (A, B, C).

prompt.en: Read the opinion column from a regional newspaper and analyse how its argument is built. (Westmere is a fictional region.)

ex.title: Sixteen at the ballot box: a case with conditions
ex.passage:
Next month, Westmere's regional council will vote on whether sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds should be allowed to vote in local elections. So far the debate has been conducted in slogans: 'Old enough to work, old enough to vote' on one side, 'Let children be children' on the other. Both deserve better arguments than they have received. My own view is that the council should say yes, but to a narrower proposal than either side imagines: votes at sixteen in local elections only, introduced as a pilot over two election cycles and paired with civic education in the final two years of school.

The case rests on a principle most of us already accept: the people who will live longest with the consequences of a decision should have a say in it, provided they can understand what they are deciding. Local councils decide on school transport, youth services, parks and the planning rules that will shape the town these teenagers grow up in. A sixteen-year-old will live with a new bus network or a closed youth centre for far longer than many of the people now voting on it.

The strongest objection is not that teenagers are foolish, and those who make it seriously never say so. It is that eighteen is not an arbitrary age. It is the point at which the law, in most respects, treats people as independent: able to sign contracts, to serve on juries and to bear full responsibility for their actions. A sixteen-year-old usually still lives at home, and critics fear that many first votes would simply echo a parent's. Lowering the voting age, on this view, breaks the link between political rights and independent adulthood, and does so for no clear gain.

Part of this is right. Legal thresholds should be consistent unless there is a good reason for an exception, and the burden of proof lies with those who want to change them. But the reason here is a relevant one. The other thresholds concern risks to oneself or binding obligations to others; voting concerns a share in decisions about a shared future. The worry about parental influence, meanwhile, proves too much: adults, too, vote under the influence of partners, employers and friends, and we do not ask them to prove their independence at the polling station. Some political scientists argue, moreover, that voting is partly a habit, and that a first vote cast while still at school, with a teacher explaining the ballot, may be more likely to be followed by a second.

A critic might reply that, once sixteen is accepted, nothing stops the age falling to fourteen. But a threshold is fixed by its reasons, not by the slope beneath it. The reasons given here, a direct stake in local decisions and the understanding that civic education can support in the final years of school, point to sixteen, not to fourteen.

None of this proves that votes at sixteen will work. That is precisely why the council should begin with a pilot, measure turnout and understanding, and decide after two elections whether to keep, extend or abandon it. A policy that admits it might be wrong is easier to trust than one that insists it cannot be.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the writer's thesis?
options: Sixteen-year-olds should be able to vote in all elections, local and national, from the next election onwards.
The voting age should stay at eighteen until independent research shows that younger voters understand local issues.
Sixteen-year-olds should vote in local elections, starting with a two-election pilot combined with civic education.
Each school should decide, after consulting its students, whether they may vote in local elections.

0.en: The writer explicitly narrows the proposal: 'local elections only', and as a pilot.

1.en: The writer supports change now, but in a limited, testable form.

3.en: Schools provide civic education in the proposal; they do not decide who votes.

explanation.en: The thesis is qualified in scope (local elections only), in time (a pilot over two election cycles) and by a condition (civic education in the final two years of school).

questions.question: Which warrant does the writer's main argument depend on?
options: The people who will live longest with the consequences of a decision should have a say in it, if they can understand it.
Teenagers are better informed about local politics than most adults, so their votes would improve the council's decisions.
Every legal age limit, including those for signing contracts and serving on juries, should be lowered to sixteen.
High turnout among young voters is the only reliable sign that a local democracy is healthy.

1.en: The writer never claims this; the argument rests on stake and understanding, not on being better informed than adults.

2.en: The writer argues that voting differs from other thresholds, so this would contradict the column.

3.en: Turnout is something the pilot should measure, not the principle that justifies the proposal.

explanation.en: 'The case rests on a principle most of us already accept ...' The writer states the warrant explicitly and adds a condition ('provided they can understand what they are deciding'), which later explains why civic education is part of the proposal.

questions.statement: The writer presents the objection about legal adulthood in a weak form so that it is easy to dismiss.

explanation.en: The writer steelmans it: 'The strongest objection is not that teenagers are foolish ...'. The objection is stated with its real reasons (eighteen as the age of legal independence, the risk of parental influence) before it is answered.

questions.question: How does the writer answer the point that eighteen is the age of legal independence?
options: By denying that any legal age limits are set at eighteen, and arguing that the law already treats sixteen-year-olds as independent.
By arguing that sixteen-year-olds are, on the whole, more mature and better informed than many adults who already vote.
By ignoring it and moving straight on to the evidence that voting is a habit formed early.
By conceding that age limits should be consistent, then arguing that voting differs from the other limits in a relevant way.

0.en: The writer accepts that these thresholds exist: 'Part of this is right.'

1.en: Maturity compared with adults is never claimed; the answer is about what kind of right voting is.

2.en: The writer engages with the objection directly before mentioning habit and turnout.

explanation.en: Concede ('Part of this is right ... the burden of proof lies with those who want to change them'), then distinguish: other thresholds concern risks to oneself or binding obligations, while voting concerns a share in a shared future. Showing that a case is relevantly different is a strong form of counter.

questions.question: When the writer says that the worry about parental influence 'proves too much', the point is that:
options: if the worry were a good reason, it would also exclude many adult voters, so it cannot single out sixteen-year-olds.
research has proved that parents influence their children's votes, so the worry is better founded than critics realise.
parents already have too much influence over the way adults vote, as well as over their teenage children.
the worry is too emotional to be answered with reasons, so the writer decides to set it aside.

1.en: 'Proves too much' is not about research. It means the reasoning, applied consistently, would lead to a conclusion nobody accepts.

2.en: The writer mentions influence on adults only to show that the objection would apply to them too, not to complain about it.

3.en: The writer answers the worry with a reason, so it is clearly not treated as unanswerable.

explanation.en: An argument 'proves too much' when, applied consistently, it would also justify a conclusion its own supporters reject: here, removing the vote from adults who are influenced by partners or employers. This dismantles the objection's warrant without denying the facts it rests on.

questions.statement: The writer claims that research has shown that voting at sixteen raises turnout later in life.

explanation.en: The claim is attributed and hedged: 'Some political scientists argue ... may be more likely'. The writer offers it as supporting reasoning, not as proof, which is why the pilot will measure turnout.

questions.question: Why, according to the writer, does accepting sixteen not commit anyone to fourteen?
options: Because fourteen-year-olds are not allowed to take part in civic education.
Because the council has already voted to rule out any voting age below sixteen in future.
Because nobody has ever seriously proposed a voting age as low as fourteen, so the worry is purely imaginary.
Because an age limit is set by the reasons for it, and the reasons given support sixteen but not fourteen.

0.en: The column links civic education to the final years of school, but it never says younger students are excluded from it.

1.en: The council has not voted yet; the writer answers the objection with reasoning, not with a decision.

2.en: The writer raises the objection as one a critic might make; the answer does not depend on whether anyone has suggested it.

explanation.en: 'A threshold is fixed by its reasons, not by the slope beneath it.' The writer anticipates a slippery-slope reply and answers it by returning to the warrant: stake plus supported understanding. These are steps 4 and 5 of a concession-rebuttal chain: anticipate, then respond.

questions.text: The final proposal is limited in scope (local elections only) and in time: it begins as a ___ that will be reviewed after two elections. (one word from the column)

feedback.en: Same idea, but the column's word is 'pilot': 'the council should begin with a pilot'.

explanation.en: 'That is precisely why the council should begin with a pilot ...' The final paragraph re-qualifies the thesis: the writer admits the policy might fail and builds a test into the proposal.

prompt.en: Read the introduction to a research paper and analyse its moves. (The Northvale Regional Library and its review are fictional.)

ex.title: Fine-free libraries: access, accountability and the evidence so far
ex.passage:
Overdue fines are among the oldest features of the public library. For generations, a small daily charge has been treated as a fair way to make sure that books come back and that shared resources stay shared. In recent years, however, a number of library systems have abolished fines altogether, arguing that they deter the very readers libraries most want to reach. Supporters describe the change as a matter of access; critics see it as a loss of accountability that will leave shelves emptier and budgets thinner.

Much of the public debate has relied on anecdote: a librarian's story of a family who stopped visiting after a large bill, or a councillor's warning that 'nobody will bring anything back'. The more systematic evidence is limited. Reports from library networks that have dropped fines, such as the Northvale Regional Library's two-year review (2023), describe more returning borrowers and little change in the share of items returned. However, most of these reports are produced by the libraries themselves, which have an interest in presenting the policy as a success. Independent studies are fewer, and they rarely separate the effect of abolishing fines from that of other changes introduced at the same time, such as automatic renewals and text reminders. What remains unclear, then, is not whether fine-free policies are popular, but whether they achieve their main aim, wider access, without the costs their critics predict.

This paper asks: to what extent does abolishing overdue fines widen access to public libraries, and at what cost to the return of materials? It argues that the available evidence supports abolishing fines for children's and young adults' materials, where the gains in access appear largest and the losses smallest, but that the case for adult collections is weaker and depends on replacing fines with other safeguards, such as automatic renewals and limits on borrowing after long delays.

The paper focuses on public lending libraries in cities and towns; it does not consider university or school libraries, whose borrowers and funding work differently. It treats 'access' as the number and range of people who borrow regularly, rather than as the number of visits, which may include people who never borrow at all.

The paper first explains how fines were justified and what 'fine-free' has meant in practice. It then examines the evidence on borrowing among low-income families, followed by the evidence on returns. Next, it considers the strongest objection: that removing the penalty removes the incentive to return books on time and shifts the cost of delays onto other borrowers. It argues that this objection is partly right for adult collections. It concludes by setting out what libraries considering the change should measure, and what remains unknown.

questions.question: Which sentence states the gap that the paper sets out to address?
options: For generations, a small daily charge has been treated as a fair way to make sure that books come back and that shared resources stay shared.
What remains unclear, then, is not whether fine-free policies are popular, but whether they achieve their main aim, wider access, without the costs their critics predict.
Supporters describe the change as a matter of access; critics see it as a loss of accountability that will leave shelves emptier and budgets thinner.
It concludes by setting out what libraries considering the change should measure, and what remains unknown.

0.en: This sets the context: why fines have been used. It does not say what the research has failed to answer.

2.en: This frames the debate; the gap comes after the writer has evaluated the evidence on each side.

3.en: This belongs to the roadmap: it says what the paper will do at the end.

explanation.en: 'What remains unclear ...' names the question that existing evidence leaves open, after the writer has explained why the available reports cannot settle it. The research question in the next paragraph answers this gap directly.

questions.question: Why does the writer treat the libraries' own reports with caution?
options: Because they were published more than ten years ago, before most libraries had changed their policies.
Because they report that return rates collapsed once borrowers no longer faced any penalty.
Because they contain no information about who borrows, so they cannot say anything about access.
Because the libraries that produced them have an interest in presenting the policy as a success.

0.en: The review named in the passage is from 2023; age is not the issue.

1.en: The reports describe 'little change in the share of items returned', not a collapse.

2.en: They describe 'more returning borrowers', so they do contain information about borrowers.

explanation.en: 'Most of these reports are produced by the libraries themselves, which have an interest in presenting the policy as a success.' This is source evaluation inside an introduction: a vested interest is a reason for caution, not for dismissal.

questions.statement: The thesis claims that fines should be abolished in every public library collection.

explanation.en: The thesis divides the claim: the evidence supports abolishing fines for children's and young adults' materials, while the case for adult collections is 'weaker' and conditional on other safeguards.

questions.statement: Under the writer's definition of 'access', a person who visits the library but never borrows would not count.

explanation.en: 'It treats access as the number and range of people who borrow regularly, rather than as the number of visits, which may include people who never borrow at all.' Defining a key term at the start fixes what the evidence must show.

questions.question: The clause 'it does not consider university or school libraries, whose borrowers and funding work differently' is:
options: a delimitation: a boundary the writer has chosen and justified.
a limitation: a weakness in the evidence that the writer cannot control.
a counterargument to the thesis.
part of the roadmap.

1.en: Nothing here is a weakness in the evidence. The writer chose to leave these libraries out, and says why.

2.en: It does not oppose the thesis; it marks where the thesis applies.

3.en: The roadmap is the final paragraph, which previews the order of the sections.

explanation.en: A delimitation is a deliberate boundary with a reason ('whose borrowers and funding work differently'). Limitations, such as the short time span of the evidence, belong near the end of the paper.

questions.text: According to the roadmap, the strongest objection is that removing the penalty removes the ___ to return books on time. (one word from the text)

feedback.en: Close in meaning, but the word in the text is 'incentive': 'removes the incentive to return books on time'.
Close in meaning, but the word in the text is 'incentive': 'removes the incentive to return books on time'.

explanation.en: 'Next, it considers the strongest objection: that removing the penalty removes the incentive to return books on time ...' Placing the objection in the roadmap shows the reader that the paper will answer the best case against it, not avoid it.

questions.question: Which description fits the thesis best?
options: Descriptive: it reports what libraries have done and what critics fear, without taking a position of its own.
Unqualified: it claims that fines should be abolished in every public library, whatever the collection.
Qualified: it divides the claim by type of collection and makes the case for adult collections conditional.
Over-hedged: it qualifies the claim so heavily that it avoids committing to any position.

0.en: It takes a clear position: the evidence 'supports abolishing fines' for some collections.

1.en: It explicitly limits the claim to children's and young adults' materials.

3.en: It commits clearly for one type of collection and states exactly what the other case depends on.

explanation.en: The thesis is limited by scope (children's and young adults' materials) and by condition (for adult collections, only if fines are replaced with other safeguards). It answers the research question directly, and it previews where the strongest objection will be partly accepted.
